019fa77d-8469-7104-aa43-56df5a5cb8fe.summary: Express numbers as products of primes in index form, then read HCF from shared primes at lowest powers and LCM from every prime at highest powers.
key_concepts: A prime is greater than 1 and divisible only by itself and 1
HCF: common bases only, take the lowest power of each
LCM: every prime that appears, take the highest power of each
For a perfect square (cube), every prime power in the factorisation must be divisible by 2 (3)

formulas.label: HCF from primes
formulas.expression: HCF = product of shared primes at lowest powers
formulas.note: Ignore primes that appear in only one number.

formulas.label: LCM from primes
formulas.expression: LCM = product of all primes at highest powers
formulas.note: Include primes found in only one of the numbers.

worked_examples.question: Find the HCF of 168 and 560.
Express 2700 as a product of primes. Find the smallest h so that 2700h is a perfect square, and the smallest k so that 2700k is a perfect cube.
steps: For a square, every power must be divisible by 2; only 3^3 needs one more factor of 3, so h = 3
For a cube, every power must be divisible by 3; need 2^1 and 5^1 more, so k = 2 x 5 = 10

common_mistakes.mistake: Taking the highest powers when finding the HCF.
common_mistakes.fix: HCF uses the lowest shared powers. Highest powers are for LCM.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaving out a prime that appears in only one number when finding the LCM.
common_mistakes.fix: LCM must include every prime that appears in either number.

exam_tips: Write both numbers in index form before comparing primes.
For square/cube questions, check which powers are not divisible by 2 or 3, then multiply by the missing factors.

019fa77d-846f-77df-b73d-aeca15ab2712.summary: Index laws let you simplify powers without expanding. Standard form keeps very large or small numbers as A x 10^n with 1 <= A < 10.
key_concepts: Same base: multiply by adding indices, divide by subtracting, and raise a power by multiplying indices
Fractional indices are roots: a^(m/n) is the nth root of a^m
Standard form is A x 10^n where 1 <= A < 10

formulas.label: Core index laws
formulas.expression: a^m x a^n = a^(m+n); a^m / a^n = a^(m-n); (a^m)^n = a^(mn)
formulas.note: Bases must match for the first two laws.

formulas.label: Negative and zero index
formulas.note: Neither law applies when a = 0.

formulas.label: Fractional index
formulas.note: Also (ab)^n = a^n b^n and (a/b)^m = a^m / b^m.

worked_examples.question: Simplify (4x^2)^(3/2).
steps: Apply (ab)^n = a^n b^n and a^(m/n) as a root: (4x^2)^(3/2) = 4^(3/2) x (x^2)^(3/2)

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating a negative index as making the answer negative.
common_mistakes.fix: A negative index flips into a reciprocal; it does not change the sign.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaving standard form as 34 x 10^5.
common_mistakes.fix: The first part must satisfy 1 <= A < 10, so write 3.4 x 10^6.

exam_tips: Rewrite nested roots and brackets fully in index form before simplifying from the inside out.
Spot zero powers early; they often collapse a messy expression to 1.

019fa77d-846f-78a5-8c08-d120beccd3ac.summary: Direct proportion means y = kx. Inverse proportion means y = k/x (or y = k over a power/root of x).
key_concepts: Direct: as one quantity increases, the other increases and y = bx for a constant b
Inverse: as one quantity increases, the other decreases and y = b/x
Find the constant from the given pair first, then substitute the new value

formulas.label: Direct proportion
formulas.note: b is the constant of proportionality.

formulas.label: Inverse proportion
formulas.note: Also used with roots or powers, e.g. L = b / sqrt(M).

worked_examples.question: y is directly proportional to x. Given y = 144 when x = 12, find y when x = 7.
steps: y = bx so 144 = b(12), giving b = 12

worked_examples.question: L is inversely proportional to sqrt(M). When M = 100, L = 35. Find M when L = 700.

common_mistakes.mistake: Skipping the step of finding the constant.
common_mistakes.fix: Always substitute the given pair to find b before answering.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using y = bx when the question says inversely proportional.
common_mistakes.fix: Inverse means y = b/x (or b over the stated expression).

exam_tips: Underline whether the question says directly or inversely proportional.
Label given and new values clearly so the constant step is easy to check.

019fa797-96d4-7182-967a-27541bebc955.summary: A map scale compares map length to actual length. Areas scale by the square of the length scale.
key_concepts: Scale = D_map / D_actual, often rewritten as the representative fraction 1 : n
Both lengths must use the same unit before writing 1 : n
A_map / A_actual = (D_map / D_actual)^2

formulas.label: Length scale
formulas.note: Reduce so the map side is 1.

formulas.label: Area scale
formulas.note: Square the length scale factor.

worked_examples.question: A map has scale 1 : 200000. (a) Write as 1 cm : n km. (b) Map distance 18.9 cm. Find actual distance in km. (c) Actual area 728.6 km^2. Find map area in cm^2.
steps: 1 cm represents 200000 cm = 2 km, so n = 2
1 cm^2 represents 2^2 = 4 km^2, so map area = 728.6 / 4 = 182.15 cm^2

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the length scale factor directly for an area.
common_mistakes.fix: Square the length scale: areas scale by n^2.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing 1 : n with mixed units.
common_mistakes.fix: Convert both lengths to the same unit before simplifying.

exam_tips: Convert 1 : n into a convenient unit pair (e.g. 1 cm : 2 km) before area work.
Check whether the question asks for length or area; that decides whether you square.

019fa77d-846f-78bf-9be6-38293f247790.summary: Percentages are fractions with denominator 100. Most exam marks come from choosing the correct 100% baseline and using multipliers.
key_concepts: Percent rate x base value = percentage amount
Increase uses (100% + rate); decrease uses (100% - rate)
Reverse percentage: final value is a known percent of the original, so divide by that multiplier

formulas.label: Percentage of a base
formulas.note: E.g. 8.5% of $7.20 is GST tax.

formulas.label: Percentage change
formulas.note: Always measure against the previous (original) value.

formulas.label: Increase / decrease multiplier
formulas.note: For reverse percentages, divide final by that multiplier.

worked_examples.question: A pair of shoes costs $17.50 after a 15% discount. Find the price before discount.
An index rises from 1267 to 1298 (a change of +31). Find the percentage increase to 3 s.f.

common_mistakes.mistake: Multiplying by 1.15 to reverse a 15% discount.
common_mistakes.fix: Divide by 0.85. Reverse percentages divide by the remaining percent.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the new value as the 100% baseline for percentage change.
common_mistakes.fix: Percentage change is always measured against the previous value.

exam_tips: Write down what represents 100% before calculating.
On a calculator, key fraction x 100 (not x 100%) when converting to a percentage.

019fa77d-846f-78da-8d36-a3c6c5093e2d.summary: Simple interest adds a fixed amount each period on the original principal. Compound interest recalculates on the new balance each period.
key_concepts: Simple interest per period is constant and based on the original principal
Compound interest amount grows each period because interest is earned on the previous total
Compound formulas usually give the final amount A; interest earned is A - P

formulas.label: Simple interest
formulas.note: R is the rate as a decimal or percent/100; T is the number of periods.

formulas.label: Compound amount
formulas.note: A is the final amount after T compounding periods.

worked_examples.question: Deposit $2300 at 3% simple interest per year. Find the interest and amount after 2 years.
Deposit $12000 at 4% compound interest per year. Find the amount after 2 years.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reporting the compound amount when the question asks for the interest.
common_mistakes.fix: Interest earned = final amount minus the principal.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using simple interest when the question says compound.
common_mistakes.fix: Compound interest multiplies by (1 + r/100) once per period.

exam_tips: Check whether the question wants the total amount or just the interest.
For simple interest, A = P(1 + RT) is often faster than finding I first.

019fa797-96d4-7391-a305-684acbf30080.subtopic_name: Exchange rates, hire purchase and taxation
019fa797-96d4-7391-a305-684acbf30080.summary: Convert currencies carefully with the given rate, and treat hire purchase as deposit plus all instalments (often with simple interest on the balance).
key_concepts: Rewrite the exchange rate so the currency you want is on the RHS before multiplying
Hire purchase total = deposit + remaining amount + interest (if charged)
Tax is charged in bands, so only the income inside each band is taxed at that band's rate

formulas.label: Currency conversion
formulas.expression: new amount = original amount x (units of new per 1 unit of old)
formulas.note: Invert the given rate if needed, then multiply.

formulas.label: Hire purchase instalment
formulas.expression: instalment = (remaining amount + total interest) / number of instalments
formulas.note: Total payable = deposit + remaining amount + interest.

worked_examples.question: 1 SGD = 0.64 EUR. A present costs 19 EUR + 11 EUR transport, plus 7 SGD import charges. Find the total in SGD.
A car costs $50000. Deposit 40%, then 24 monthly instalments with 2.5% simple interest on the remaining amount. Find the monthly instalment and total payable.

common_mistakes.mistake: Multiplying when you should divide in a currency conversion.
common_mistakes.fix: Sanity-check the size, or rewrite the rate so the target currency is on the RHS.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the deposit or the interest when totalling hire purchase.
common_mistakes.fix: Total = deposit + remaining balance + interest charged.

common_mistakes.mistake: Taxing the whole income at the highest band rate.
common_mistakes.fix: Only the part of the income inside a band is taxed at that band's rate.

exam_tips: Write the exchange rate as a fraction and cancel units.
Hire purchase always costs at least as much as cash (usually more); use that as a check.

019fa77e-4a20-77c9-9dbd-84e3b0a7ecaf.summary: Expand by multiplying every term; factorise by extracting common factors or recognising identities. Only like terms can be combined.
key_concepts: Only like terms can be added or subtracted (e.g. 2x + 3x = 5x)
Expand by multiplying the outside term (or each term) through every term in the bracket
Factorisation reverses expansion: take out the HCF, use identities, grouping, or the cross method

formulas.label: Perfect square and difference of squares
formulas.note: Spot these before using the general rainbow/FOIL method.

worked_examples.question: Expand (3x + 5)^2 and (x + 5)(x - 5).
Factorise completely 49 - 4x^2 and 2a^2 - 8a.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing (a + b)^2 as a^2 + b^2.
common_mistakes.fix: Include the middle term 2ab.

common_mistakes.mistake: Combining unlike terms such as 3x and 5.
common_mistakes.fix: Only like terms (same letters and powers) can be added or subtracted.

exam_tips: Expand your factorised answer mentally to check it.
Completely usually means take out a common factor and then factorise further.

019fa77e-4a20-7a03-898c-3b69d3499409.subtopic_name: Algebraic fractions and changing the subject
019fa77e-4a20-7a03-898c-3b69d3499409.summary: Combine algebraic fractions over a common denominator, and rearrange formulas so the required letter stands alone on the LHS.
key_concepts: Factorise denominators before finding a common denominator; cancel factors only
Changing the subject means isolating one letter alone on the LHS
Square roots give +/- answers unless the context (e.g. distance) rejects the negative

formulas.label: Adding fractions
formulas.note: Simplify the result if possible.

worked_examples.question: Make c the subject of E = mc^2.
steps: Divide both sides by m: E/m = c^2
Square root both sides: c = +/- sqrt(E/m)

worked_examples.question: Make m the subject of E = (1/2)mv^2.

common_mistakes.mistake: Cancelling the x in (x + 3)/x.
common_mistakes.fix: Only cancel a factor common to the whole numerator and denominator.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropping the +/- when taking a square root in changing the subject.
common_mistakes.fix: Include both signs unless the question rejects negatives (e.g. length).

exam_tips: Undo operations in reverse order: clear fractions, isolate the powered term, then take roots.
When the new subject appears twice, collect those terms and factorise it out.

019fa77e-4a20-7a3a-8806-6eebbef428fd.summary: Every non-vertical straight line can be written as y = mx + c, where m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept.
key_concepts: Gradient m = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1); a vertical line has undefined gradient
c is the value of y when x = 0
Parallel lines share the same gradient

formulas.label: Gradient from two points
formulas.note: Keep the order of subtraction consistent.

formulas.label: Equation of a line
formulas.note: If the line is vertical, write it as x = k.

worked_examples.question: A is (3, -5) and B is (-1, -9). Find the equation of line AB.

common_mistakes.mistake: Computing gradient as change in x over change in y.
common_mistakes.fix: Gradient is change in y over change in x.

common_mistakes.mistake: Mixing the order of points in numerator and denominator.
common_mistakes.fix: If you start with point 2 on top, start with point 2 on the bottom too.

exam_tips: Rearrange given equations into y = mx + c to read the gradient quickly.
Read the axis scales carefully before measuring a gradient off a graph.

019fa77e-4a20-7a59-a2f1-9b582ffbba2f.summary: Recognise graph shapes from equations. For quadratics, the line of symmetry passes through the turning point (minimum or maximum).
key_concepts: a > 0 gives a U-shaped quadratic (minimum); a < 0 gives an n-shape (maximum)
Line of symmetry is midway between the roots; turning point lies on it
Completed-square form y = (x - h)^2 + k shows the turning point (h, k) directly
Other shapes: cubic, reciprocal y = a/x (axes as asymptotes), exponential y = a^x

formulas.label: Completed square form
formulas.note: Turning point is (h, k).

formulas.label: Reciprocal graph
formulas.note: Does not meet the axes; a < 0 reflects into other quadrants.

worked_examples.question: For y = -(x - 5)(x + 1), find the x-intercepts, y-intercept, turning point and line of symmetry.
steps: Roots when y = 0: x = 5 or x = -1, so intercepts (5, 0) and (-1, 0)
Line of symmetry x = 2; maximum at (2, 9) since a < 0

worked_examples.question: Express x^2 - 4x + 5 in the form (x - h)^2 + k.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading the turning point of (x - 2)^2 + 1 as (-2, 1).
common_mistakes.fix: The x-coordinate is +2; the sign inside the bracket flips.

common_mistakes.mistake: Joining plotted points with straight lines on a curve.
common_mistakes.fix: Draw a single smooth curve through the points.

exam_tips: Identify the shape from the equation before plotting.
Label axes and write the equation beside each sketch.

019fa77e-4a20-7a72-9313-8026d7faa4f5.summary: Solve inequalities like equations, but reverse the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative.
key_concepts: Do the same operation to both sides
Adding/subtracting, or multiplying/dividing by a positive, keeps the inequality sign
Multiplying or dividing by a negative flips the inequality sign
On a number line: hollow circle for < or >; filled circle for <= or >=

formulas.label: Sign reversal rule
formulas.note: Dividing by -2 flips < to >.

worked_examples.question: Solve (-1/4)x >= 12.
steps: Multiply both sides by -4 and flip the sign

common_mistakes.mistake: Keeping the inequality sign the same after dividing by a negative.
common_mistakes.fix: Reverse the sign whenever you multiply or divide by a negative number.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a filled circle for a strict inequality on a number line.
common_mistakes.fix: Hollow circle means excluded (< or >); filled means included (<= or >=).

exam_tips: After solving, test one value from your range to confirm it works.
Compound inequalities like 10 < x <= 20 mean both ends apply at once.

019fa77e-4a20-7c37-92ed-92b483c805c2.summary: Two unknowns need two equations (elimination or substitution). Quadratics need factorising, the formula, or completing the square, and context may reject some roots.
key_concepts: Elimination when coefficients can be matched; substitution when one variable is already isolated
A quadratic must be in the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 before solving
In applications, reject roots that are impossible (e.g. negative rates or distances)

formulas.label: Quadratic formula
formulas.note: For ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with a != 0.

worked_examples.question: Solve 2x - 5y = -1 and 6x - 4y = 30 by elimination.
Solve 3x^2 - 30x - 5000 = 0 to 2 d.p. (pump rate; reject impossible roots).

common_mistakes.mistake: Trying to factorise a quadratic that has not been rearranged to equal zero.
common_mistakes.fix: Move every term to one side so the equation reads ... = 0 first.

common_mistakes.mistake: Giving only one solution to a quadratic.
common_mistakes.fix: State both roots, then reject any that fail the context check.

exam_tips: If answers are needed to 2 decimal places, use the quadratic formula.
Substitute both answers back into an original equation to check.

019fa77f-0ed2-7580-a556-eae0ff73494a.summary: Sets group elements. Read the symbols carefully, then shade the matching region on a Venn diagram.
key_concepts: Intersection (A intersect B) is elements in both; union (A union B) is elements in either
A' is the complement: elements of the universal set not in A
A intersect B = empty set means the sets are disjoint (no overlap)
n(A) is the number of elements in A

formulas.label: Union count
formulas.expression: n(A union B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A intersect B)
formulas.note: Subtract the overlap so it is not counted twice.

formulas.label: Complement
formulas.note: Universal set is often written as epsilon.

worked_examples.question: With dummy sets epsilon = {1..10}, A = {2,3,4,5}, B = {4,5,6,7,8,9}, list A intersect B and describe (A intersect B')'.
steps: (A intersect B')' is everything except {2,3}, i.e. {1,4,5,6,7,8,9,10}
worked_examples.answer: A intersect B = {4,5}; shaded region is all except A-only

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding n(A) and n(B) without subtracting the overlap.
common_mistakes.fix: Elements in both sets would be counted twice. Subtract the intersection.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing the union and intersection symbols.
common_mistakes.fix: Union looks like a cup and collects everything; intersection is the overlap only.

exam_tips: For shading questions, invent temporary dummy elements, shade, then erase them.
Fill the intersection of a Venn diagram first, then work outwards.

019fa77f-0ed2-76b8-9b76-1055b754a2df.summary: Matrices store data in rows and columns. Addition needs matching order; multiplication needs the columns of the first to equal the rows of the second.
key_concepts: Order is rows x columns; a square matrix has equal rows and columns
Add/subtract entry by entry only when orders match; scalar multiplies every entry
For AB, columns of A must equal rows of B; result has order (rows of A) x (columns of B)
AB is usually not the same as BA

formulas.label: Order of a matrix
formulas.note: Always state rows first.

formulas.label: Multiplication dimensions
formulas.expression: (m x n) x (n x p) = (m x p)
formulas.note: Inner numbers must match.

worked_examples.question: Andy buys 5 pencils, 6 pens, 2 erasers; Mark buys 8, 4, 0. Costs are $0.20, $1.50, $0.40. Form matrices and find each total spend.
worked_examples.answer: (10.80 / 7.60); totals spent by Andy and Mark

common_mistakes.mistake: Multiplying matrices element by element.
common_mistakes.fix: Multiply each row of the first by each column of the second, then add.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming AB equals BA.
common_mistakes.fix: Matrix multiplication is not commutative. Keep the given order.

exam_tips: Write the dimensions above each matrix before multiplying to check it is possible.
For interpretation questions, state what a row and a column represent in context.

019fa77f-0ed2-7889-a1bc-441d9ff8f55c.summary: Congruent triangles are the same shape and size. Similar triangles have the same shape with corresponding sides in proportion.
key_concepts: Congruence tests: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS (state the test used)
Similarity tests: AAA (two equal angles suffice), SSS sides proportional, SAS sides proportional with included equal angle
Congruent uses the symbol ≡; similar figures share shape but not necessarily size

formulas.label: Length scale factor
formulas.expression: k = corresponding length on larger / corresponding length on smaller
formulas.note: Match corresponding sides carefully.

formulas.label: Area and volume scaling
formulas.expression: area ratio = k^2; volume ratio = k^3
formulas.note: Already standard for similar figures; square/cube the length factor.

worked_examples.question: State which congruence rule applies when two triangles have two equal sides and the included equal angle.
steps: Two corresponding sides equal with the included angle equal

worked_examples.question: Two similar solids have heights 4 cm and 10 cm. The smaller has volume 32 cm^3. Find the volume of the larger.

common_mistakes.mistake: Claiming congruence from AAA alone.
common_mistakes.fix: AAA proves similarity, not congruence; sizes may differ.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the length scale factor directly for area or volume.
common_mistakes.fix: Square it for area and cube it for volume.

exam_tips: Sketch both triangles the same way round before pairing sides.
In proofs, name the triangles in corresponding vertex order and state the test (e.g. SAS).

019fa780-0e84-7e60-b2fc-65a592509a11.summary: In a right-angled triangle, use Pythagoras for three sides and SOHCAHTOA when an angle is involved.
key_concepts: Hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the right angle
Label opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse relative to the angle you are using
Use inverse sin/cos/tan to find an angle from two sides

formulas.label: Pythagoras theorem
formulas.note: c is the hypotenuse.

formulas.label: SOHCAHTOA
formulas.expression: sin = O/H; cos = A/H; tan = O/A
formulas.note: Choose the ratio that uses the two sides you know.

worked_examples.question: In a right-angled triangle, opposite = 3, adjacent = 4, hypotenuse = 5. Find the angle theta opposite the side of length 3.
steps: Known opposite and hypotenuse, so use sine

common_mistakes.mistake: Using Pythagoras when one of the given values is an angle.
common_mistakes.fix: Pythagoras only relates three sides. Use trigonometry when an angle appears.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaving the calculator in radian mode.
common_mistakes.fix: Set the calculator to degrees before any trigonometry.

exam_tips: Label O, A and H relative to your chosen angle before picking a ratio.
Check the hypotenuse is the longest side in your answer.

019fa780-0e85-712d-a090-4b3d82b18a9b.summary: The Cartesian plane uses perpendicular x- and y-axes meeting at the origin (0, 0). Points, midpoints and distances are the basic tools.
key_concepts: A point is written (x, y); the origin is (0, 0)
Read scales carefully: each small square may represent 1 unit or a fraction of a unit
Distance between two points comes from Pythagoras on the coordinate differences
Midpoint is the average of the x-coordinates and of the y-coordinates

formulas.label: Midpoint
formulas.note: Average each coordinate separately.

formulas.label: Distance
formulas.note: Same as length of the line segment joining the points.

worked_examples.question: A point is 4 units left of the origin and 7 units above it. State its coordinates.
steps: Left of the origin means negative x
Above the origin means positive y

worked_examples.question: Find the distance between A(3, -5) and B(-1, -9).

common_mistakes.mistake: Subtracting coordinates when finding a midpoint.
common_mistakes.fix: Midpoint means average: add and divide by two.

common_mistakes.mistake: Misreading the grid scale when plotting or reading a point.
common_mistakes.fix: Check what each small square represents before reading coordinates.

exam_tips: Always label the x-axis and y-axis on sketches.
Plot points roughly to sanity-check distance and midpoint answers.

019fa780-0e85-714b-8123-58667f21b215.summary: A vector has magnitude and direction. Add by the triangle/parallelogram law, and use column vectors for components.
key_concepts: Vector AB means go from A to B; BA = -AB
Triangle law: AB + BC = AC; subtract by adding the negative
Parallel vectors are scalar multiples; collinear points have AB = k AC
Magnitude of column vector (x / y) is sqrt(x^2 + y^2)

formulas.label: Magnitude
formulas.note: For the column vector (x / y).

formulas.label: Displacement
formulas.expression: AB = position of B - position of A
formulas.note: Destination minus start.

worked_examples.question: A is (-9, 2) and BA = (8 / -6). Find |BA|, the coordinates of B, and m if CD = (m / -3) is parallel to BA.
steps: Position of A - BA = position of B: (-9 / 2) - (8 / -6) = (-17 / 8), so B = (-17, 8)

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing AB as a - b when OA = a and OB = b.
common_mistakes.fix: AB = b - a (end minus start).

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding magnitudes to get the magnitude of a sum.
common_mistakes.fix: Add the components first, then apply the magnitude formula.

exam_tips: Draw arrows on the diagram for every vector you write down.
If two vectors are parallel, write one as k times the other and solve for k.

019fa780-0e85-71ab-b016-3c60cee766c0.summary: Mean, median and mode summarise a data set differently. Range is the simplest measure of spread for ungrouped data.
key_concepts: Mean = sum of observations / number of observations
Mode is the most frequent value
Median is the middle value after ordering; for an even count, average the two middle values
Range = largest value - smallest value

formulas.label: Mean (ungrouped)
formulas.note: N is the number of observations.

formulas.label: Median position (odd N)
formulas.note: For even N, average the values at N/2 and N/2 + 1.

worked_examples.question: Find the median of 9, 5, 3, 1, 2.
Find the median of 2, 4, 8, 10, 12, 15.

common_mistakes.mistake: Finding the median without ordering the data.
common_mistakes.fix: Always sort into ascending order first.

common_mistakes.mistake: Calling every common value a mode without checking frequency.
common_mistakes.fix: The mode is the value that appears most often.

exam_tips: State whether you used mean, median or mode, and give units when relevant.
If outliers matter, the median is usually more representative than the mean.

019fa799-85bc-7e0f-b6c8-3e8869a04a9e.subtopic_name: Standard deviation and comparing data sets
019fa799-85bc-7e0f-b6c8-3e8869a04a9e.summary: Standard deviation measures spread about the mean. Use mean and SD together to compare two data sets in context.
key_concepts: Larger SD means values are more spread out / less consistent
For grouped data, use class mid-points with frequencies
Compare average (mean) and spread (SD) separately, using the question context

formulas.label: SD (ungrouped)
formulas.note: Equivalent to sqrt(mean of squares - square of mean).

formulas.label: Mean and SD (grouped)
formulas.expression: mean = sum(fx)/sum(f); s.d. = sqrt( sum(f x^2)/sum(f) - (mean)^2 )
formulas.note: x is the mid-point of each class. Write 'standard deviation' in full in answers.

worked_examples.question: Find the standard deviation of 5, 0, 9, 7, 2.
Grouped marks with mid-points 55,65,75,85,95 and frequencies 15,28,18,13,8. Find mean and SD.
steps: s.d. = sqrt( mean of squares - square of mean ) ≈ 12.2 (3 s.f.)

common_mistakes.mistake: Subtracting in the wrong order inside the square root.
common_mistakes.fix: It is mean of the squares minus the square of the mean (never negative).

common_mistakes.mistake: Comparing two data sets using the mean alone.
common_mistakes.fix: Mention both the average and the spread for full marks.

exam_tips: Set out a table of mid-point x, f, fx and f x^2 before substituting.
A smaller standard deviation means more consistent results in context.

019fa799-85bc-7e8f-847b-a45e098e814a.subtopic_name: Statistical diagrams and cumulative frequency curves
019fa799-85bc-7e8f-847b-a45e098e814a.summary: Frequency tables and diagrams organise data. A cumulative frequency curve gives median and quartiles by reading across and down.
key_concepts: Grouped frequency tables use class intervals; read inequality signs carefully when tallying
A cumulative frequency curve plots running total against the upper class boundary
Median at n/2; lower quartile at n/4; upper quartile at 3n/4 on the vertical axis

formulas.label: Median position on CF curve
formulas.note: n is the total frequency.

formulas.label: Quartile positions
formulas.note: IQR = UQ - LQ.

worked_examples.question: A cumulative frequency curve covers 200 students. Explain how to find the median and how many scored more than 70.
steps: For the median, read across from 100 on the CF axis to the curve, then down to the marks axis
For scores above 70, read up from 70 to find how many scored 70 or less
worked_examples.answer: Median at CF = 100; number above 70 = 200 - CF reading at 70

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading the median halfway along the marks axis.
common_mistakes.fix: Read at half the total frequency on the vertical (CF) axis.

common_mistakes.mistake: Plotting cumulative frequency against the class midpoint.
common_mistakes.fix: Plot against the upper class boundary.

common_mistakes.mistake: Misreading class inequalities when building a frequency table.
common_mistakes.fix: Check whether the interval uses < or <= before tallying.

exam_tips: Draw reading lines onto the graph to show your method.
Check the curve finishes at the total frequency.
